analysis.one_liner: Bans pricing algorithms trained on competitors' private data and requires firms to disclose algorithm-set prices.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2024 with 6 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful to use or sell pricing software that was trained with nonpublic data from competitors, the practice behind several known price-fixing schemes in hotels, rentals, and other markets. It would let the FTC and Justice Department demand a report from any company about how its pricing algorithms work, with executive certification under penalty of perjury. It would create a legal presumption that a seller and its rivals using the same pricing tool have illegally agreed to fix prices, and require large firms to tell customers and workers when an algorithm sets their price or pay. It would also order the FTC to study how widely such algorithms are used.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy things priced by algorithms — renters, travelers, online shoppers — and workers whose pay is set algorithmically, since the bill defines 'price' to include employee and contractor compensation. Everyone who benefits when a market's prices reflect competition rather than a shared software tool that keeps prices aligned at a higher level.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to use or distribute any pricing algorithm that uses, incorporates, or was trained with nonpublic competitor data, enforceable by the FTC or Justice Department with civil penalties of at least $10,000 per day or the total sales made through the violating algorithm.

Creates an enforcement audit: on request, a company must submit a report within 30 days explaining how its pricing algorithm works, what data it uses and where it came from, whether it discriminates between customers or between workers, and whether a third party built it — certified by a senior executive under penalty of perjury.

Sets a legal presumption that a seller has entered an illegal price-fixing agreement when a pricing algorithm is distributed to two or more sellers in the same market, shifting the burden onto the defendant and imposing joint and several liability on distributors that knew or should have known the tool used competitors' nonpublic data.

Requires firms with $5 million or more in annual revenue to tell customers before purchase, and tell employees and independent contractors, that a pricing algorithm set or recommended their price or pay, and to disclose price discrimination and the identity of third-party algorithm providers.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the costs would fall on companies that sell or use pricing and revenue-management software — hotels, airlines, rental property managers, online retailers, and the software vendors serving them — in penalties, compliance reporting, and lost revenue from algorithms no longer allowed to train on rivals' private data.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pricing-software vendors and large algorithm users

drawbacks.text: The prohibition is strict and broad: it bans any algorithm trained with 'nonpublic competitor data,' a category that reaches beyond overt collusion to data flows that many ordinary market-data services provide, which could sweep in common dynamic-pricing practices that actually lower prices, such as airline yield management.

The bill creates a presumption of a Sherman Act price-fixing agreement — normally requiring proof of an actual deal — whenever a pricing tool is used by two or more sellers in a market, exposing neutral software vendors and their customers to joint and several liability, and the rebuttal requires the demanding standard of clear and convincing evidence.

Because the ban only reaches algorithms trained on nonpublic competitor data, firms could lawfully continue pricing algorithms trained on public or aggregated data, so the most widespread forms of algorithm-driven price alignment would remain untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Algorithmic price-fixing is a real and documented harm, and existing antitrust law struggles with it because the 'agreement' happens inside shared software rather than in a meeting. This bill targets that gap directly and adds transparency for consumers and workers. The trade-off is that the ban and the presumption of collusion are drafted broadly enough to reach legitimate dynamic pricing and impose real compliance costs on firms far smaller than the price-fixers the bill describes. A narrower version targeting shared, rivals-data-trained tools — the known harm — with more precision would capture most of the benefit at less cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or moved it, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the Preventing Algorithmic Collusion Act of 2024 on January 30, 2024, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Senators Wyden, Durbin, Blumenthal, Hirono, and Welch.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, the only action it ever received.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and with the 118th Congress ending January 3, 2025, the bill expired without any vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that sell and use pricing algorithms trained on competitors' private data keep the status quo: no prohibition, no mandatory audit reports, and no disclosure requirements. Consumers and workers priced or paid by such algorithms gain nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pricing-software vendors and their large users

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.role: U.S. Senator from Minnesota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its ban on pricing algorithms trained with nonpublic competitor data.

for.name: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Sponsor and cosponsors (Klobuchar, Wyden, Durbin, Blumenthal, Hirono, Welch)

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the remainder of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats — 6 of 48 Senate Democrats — and no Republican joined the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan support typically needed to move in a Senate where the majority held 48 seats plus allies.

industries.note: The bill bans distributing or selling algorithms trained with competitors' nonpublic data, creates joint and several liability for vendors, and would force disclosure of their identities to customers. These vendors profit by aligning prices across rivals in a market, which tends to raise prices for consumers above competitive levels.

industries.industry: Hotels, airlines, and short-term rental operators
industries.note: Heavy users of dynamic pricing software, they would face penalties, mandatory algorithm audit reports, and consumer disclosure requirements, and would lose the higher aligned prices that shared pricing tools can produce.

industries.industry: Rental property managers and landlords using rent-setting software
industries.note: Rent-setting algorithms trained on nonpublic competitor data would become unlawful, and the bill's transparency rules would require telling tenants that an algorithm set their rent and disclosing price discrimination.

industries.industry: Large retailers and e-commerce platforms ($5M+ revenue)
industries.note: They would bear new compliance costs — disclosure to customers, audit reports on request, executive certification — but firms whose algorithms were not trained on rivals' nonpublic data could keep operating, and retailers that compete on genuinely lower algorithmic prices could gain relative to rivals that colluded.

Because the bill defines 'price' to include pay for employees and independent contractors, platforms that set contractor pay by algorithm would have to disclose that fact and any pay differentiation among workers doing similar work, and could face liability if their pay tools were trained on competitors' nonpublic data.
